opus-5.5.text:
Oh, enormously. Irene was really one of the founders of the whole field of computer-supported cooperative work. She actually coined that term, CSCW, back in the eighties. When I joined her group at IBM Research in Cambridge, I came in as somebody who thought about visualization mostly as a one-person activity: you, a screen, and a data set, trying to make sense of it. Irene's view was that this misses most of what actually happens. People make sense of the world together. They argue, they point at things, they say "look at this," they build on each other's observations.

That reframing was a big part of what led Fernanda Viégas and me to build Many Eyes. The idea was that a visualization isn't just an endpoint for analysis. It can be a conversation starter, a social object. You put a chart on the web, someone notices a strange spike, someone else explains it, and a third person brings in another data set. What we saw was that people used visualizations to tell stories, make jokes, and make political arguments, all sorts of things a single-user mindset would never have predicted.

It also shaped how I think about the people side of technology more generally. Irene was always asking: who is actually using this, what are they trying to do with each other, and how does the tool change the social dynamics? That question has followed me into my more recent work on machine learning and interpretability. Even when you're looking inside a neural network, you're building tools for communities of people trying to understand something hard together. And honestly, the relationship between people and AI systems is itself becoming a kind of collaboration, so Irene's questions feel more relevant now than ever.

r001.rationale: The response presents people making sense of the world together—arguing, pointing things out, and building on observations—as central to Greif’s view of computer use.

fable-5.1.text:
Irene really shaped how I think about this, and in a way that I didn't fully appreciate at the time. I worked with her at IBM Research, where she ran the Collaborative User Experience group in Cambridge, and the whole premise of that group was Irene's idea. She'd coined the term "computer-supported cooperative work" back in the eighties, and the core insight was deceptively simple: computers aren't just tools that one person uses alone. People use them together, and the interesting questions are social as much as technical.

What that did for me was change where I looked for problems. I'd come to visualization thinking of it as a kind of perceptual engineering problem: how do you map data onto pixels so one viewer sees the pattern? Irene's framing pushed me to ask, what happens when a group is looking at the same picture? What do they say to each other? Who gets to annotate it, who gets to argue with it? Work like Many Eyes, which Fernanda Viégas and I built, came directly out of that. The idea that visualization could be a medium for conversation, that the comments around a chart might matter as much as the chart, that's an Irene idea at heart.

There's also a more subtle thing I took from her, which is a kind of humility about users. Irene always insisted you go observe how people actually collaborate before you build anything, because they'll surprise you. Half of what's interesting about a system is what people do with it that you didn't intend. When I was studying things like Wikipedia editing histories, I was essentially applying that lens: don't assume you know what cooperation looks like, go look at the traces people leave behind.

And honestly, I think that perspective is more relevant now than ever. We talk about AI systems as if there's one user and one model in a room, but in reality these things sit inside organizations, inside conversations, inside communities. The question of how people use these systems together is going to be the one that matters.

r001.rationale: The response identifies people using computers together and the social dynamics of their collaboration as central to Greif’s perspective.

astra-6.text:
Irene really helped me think about computing as a social activity. It’s easy to imagine a person sitting in front of a computer, doing a task, and to make that the whole picture. Her perspective encouraged me to ask: Who else is involved? Who are they communicating with? How does the work fit into what a group is trying to do?

That’s been especially useful in thinking about visualization. A visualization isn’t just something one person looks at to get an insight. It can become something people discuss, question, and use to explain their thinking to each other. So you start caring not only about whether someone can read a chart, but about whether it helps people have a productive conversation. That shift—from an individual interaction to people making sense of something together—has been a big influence on my thinking.

r001.rationale: The response presents computing as a social activity and focuses on how people communicate, collaborate, and make sense of visualizations together, identifying group dynamics as central to Greif’s influence.

sol-6.1.text: Irene had a big influence on me. She helped me think about computing as something people do together, rather than just an interaction between one person and a machine. That changes the questions you ask about visualization. You’re not only asking, “Can someone understand this data?” You’re asking, “Can they use it to explain something to another person? Can they discuss it, disagree about it, and build an understanding together?” That social side became a really important part of how I thought about the work.

r001.rationale: The response describes Irene’s perspective as treating computing as something people do together, emphasizing how people explain, discuss, disagree, and build understanding with one another.
